newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals -- Magnesium firms on European demand.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals -- Magnesium firms on European demand.

text.p: Chinese magnesium prices continued to climb in Asia, helped by demand from Europe, which is developing a taste for low-priced Chinese metal, minor metal traders said on Tuesday.

"Since May, China has been shipping more and more magnesium to Europe. Its monthly sales must stand at around 1,500 tonnes," said one trader. "If European demand remains strong in the July-September quarter, prices will rise further."
Traders said China would not sell magnesium to Japan unless Japanese buyers raised their offers to European levels.
Offers edged up to $2,400-$2,600 per tonne.
European demand for magnesium is not growing drastically, although China's market share is rising because its prices are below those for Russian supplies, traders said.
One trader, who recently visited China, estimated the country was now producing around 40,000 tonnes of magnesium per year, while output capacity has fallen to around 50,000 tonnes.

Asked about Japanese demand, the first magnesium trader said: "Domestic demand will probably peak in the second quarter when beverage can makers prepare for the summer. We haven't yet seen many signs of a decline."

Earlier today, the Japan Aluminum Federation said output of aluminium can stock at Japan's seven leading mills stood at 38,895 tonnes in May, down 2.2 percent from April but up 5.9 percent compared with the same month in 1996.
Traders in China said bismuth prices were taking a break from their breathtaking climb a month ago.
Chinese material was offered in a range of $3.75 to $3.95 a lb inclusive of cost and freight (C&F) basis Rotterdam, trading sources in both southern and northern China said.
"Generally we think it is taking a break and that it has the potential to go higher," the south China source said.
The upcoming seasonal slump in Europe would probably keep prices flat in the next few months, but demand will pick up after that and prices could rise to $4, he added.
Rhodium remained strong at around $380 per ounce as end-users were hurriedly snapping up the metal.
"Worried that the panic in the platinum and palladium...may spill over into rhodium prices, end-users were rushing to buy the metal," a precious metal industry source said.

In the cobalt market, prices eased further in a move seen instigated by some traders after Laurent Kabila last month took power in the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, which is one of the world's largest cobalt producers.

"I hear of very cheap offers by Europeans," said one trader at a major Japanese trading house. "But Japanese users are waiting as they expect prices to ease a little further. The dollar might also fall after the Denver G7 summit," he said. A weaker dollar against the yen makes imports into Japan cheaper.

Traders said they saw little scope for a further decline from the current $22.00-23.00 per pound for high-grade cobalt and the $19.00-20.00 for low-grade metal amid uncertainties over sales by the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency.

In New York on Friday, a lawyer for the government agency said two separate cases with Minor Metals Inc, which led to the suspension of U.S. stockpile cobalt sales, looked set to drag on with no clear timetable for a final outcome.

The price for molybdenum oxide was soft at $4.50/80 per pound as there was little demand from Japan following rounds of purchases over the last few months and market talk that U.S. Molycorp would resume production at one of its mines shortly.
"The price might ease towards $4. Yet I'm not worried about a collapse as we expect steady demand from steel makers," a Japanese trader said.
Chinese antimony producers were heard offering their material at $2,080 per tonne. With Western material offered around $2,000/2,000 C&F Rotterdam, he was waiting for the Chinese to find the market.
-- Lynne O'Donnell, Shanghai Newsroom (8621) 6279-8544.
-- Keiko Takagi/Nao Nakanishi, Tokyo Commodities Desk +81-3-3432-7431
